Modern bullfighting, a fight between a man on foot and a bull, took shape in Spain in the 1700s. Before it, bull-baiting and mounted bull fights were mostly a sport of nobles, who speared the bull from horseback. The Bourbon kings, starting with Philip V, are said to have lost interest, and commoners took over the ring on foot, with a cape and a sword.

The town of Ronda in the south became the centre. Francisco Romero is credited with the red cape (muleta) and the killing sword around the 1720s, and his grandson Pedro Romero fought for decades, reportedly without once being gored. By the 1800s the corrida had set rules and star matadors, and spread to France, Portugal, Mexico and Peru.

Fame brought risk. Joselito and Juan Belmonte, rivals from about 1914 to 1920, are said to have made it a high art, and Joselito was gored to death in 1920. In 1947 the great Manolete was gored by a bull named Islero at Linares and died the next day.

It became a symbol of Spanish identity and of Hispanic culture. It is also condemned for cruelty to animals and has been banned in Catalonia (later overturned) and in a number of countries.
